preamble: Wordplay in 15 clues lacks something crucial in one form or another

clue.text: Make less iron, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to reduce in amount or size
ironing a shirt takes out its creases; iron is one way of doing that

explanation.surface: An instruction to use less of the household iron, or perhaps to cut back on iron in the diet.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as DE-CREASE, to remove creases, which is what ironing does.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to reduce something is to make it smaller or fewer.

clue.text: Went off, you might say, for a number of years

indicators.note: signals that the word is spoken aloud and a soundalike is entered

parts.note: food that has gone off has rotted or decayed

explanation.surface: Someone left, or something spoiled, after a stretch of years.
explanation.walkthrough: DECAYED, said aloud, sounds like the ten-year span.
explanation.definitionFit: A ten-year period is a specific count of years.

clue.text: State arbitrators have seized some of this puzzle's content?

indicators.note: the referees hold the state's abbreviation between their letters

parts.note: referees settle disputes and decide matches
NC is North Carolina, a US state

explanation.surface: State-appointed arbitrators have confiscated part of the material in this crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the preamble's fifteen clues: the wordplay alone falls short by the word that means angry or a crucifix, which the solver restores at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: This puzzle links several lights to one another with 'See 21'-style pointers, a kind of internal pointer between entries.

clue.text: Cricket team making opposing players run back and forth

indicators.note: the two pairs of players read the same in either direction, one run followed by its mirror

parts.note: at bridge East plays against South, so ES and SE are pairs of opponents

explanation.surface: A cricket side makes the other team scamper up and down the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: ES then SE gives ESSE; the preamble's missing cross, X, completes it. 'run' joins the pieces. ESSEX is an English county with a first-class cricket side.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the county side of Essex plays first-class cricket in England.

clue.text: Musical's essential element

parts.note: the chemical symbol Si sits right inside the word musical, so this element is 'essential' to it

explanation.surface: What a stage show cannot do without.
explanation.walkthrough: Si, the symbol for this element, is found in muSIcal; 'essential' usually means a central letter, so it is loose but fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical element whose symbol Si appears within the word musical.

clue.text: One article carried by climbers primarily?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the article is held within the spelt-out letter

parts.note: the first letter of climbers is C, written out as its name, cee
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A single item that mountaineers mainly take with them.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside CEE (the letter C spelt out) after I, giving ICEAE; the preamble's missing X is restored before the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Mountaineers carry this tool for cutting steps and arresting falls on ice.

clue.text: Combining two different styles shows some balls

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end

explanation.surface: A performer mixing two genres displays some daring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balls' slangs as courage in the surface, but it is six deliveries in cricket; the preamble's missing CROSS goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A fusion of two genres, such as country with pop, is a common term in music.

clue.text: Having contrary understanding of what might be a super 19

indicators.note: asks what the letters could be rearranged into

parts.note: taken as written
the answer to 19 down is a word meaning see

explanation.surface: Two people misunderstanding each other over what might count as a great spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what might be' is the anagram signal. The preamble's missing piece, the word for a crucifix, sits in the middle of the rearranged phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: people who misunderstand each other's aims are working towards different goals.

clue.text: Recording disc certain to generate publicity

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
O is round like a disc
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A recorded single that is guaranteed to get attention.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the preamble's fifteen: the wordplay lacks the letter shaped like a cross, which goes in second place.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: coverage in the media puts someone before the public eye.

clue.text: Such a tyre goes soft? Extremely likely

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

indicators.note: the outermost letters of the next word are taken

explanation.surface: A worried question about whether a tyre goes flat, answered 'very probably'.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the preamble's fifteen: the word for a crucifix is missing from the wordplay and goes at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre construction with cords running diagonally across one another.

clue.text: A poet caught out, being a bit of a heel? Quite the opposite

definitions.text: a bit of a heel? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order, rearranged

parts.note: c is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A poet exposed as something of a cad, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges A POET and C. 'heel' suggests a cad; it is the back of a shoe, and the answer is at the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: The reinforced front of a boot covers the toes, the opposite end of the footwear from the rear.

clue.text: Not one of the 21 formerly used for counterirritant

parts.note: the moa was a flightless New Zealand bird, now extinct, so not one of the fliers of 21 down, and only in the past

explanation.surface: Something no longer used as a remedy, unlike the items at 21.
explanation.walkthrough: The moa was a flightless New Zealand bird, now extinct. The preamble's missing letter shaped like a cross belongs in third place, before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A downy plant material burnt on the skin in traditional medicine to relieve pain elsewhere.

clue.text: Castrate last of brood — Siamese not seeing Thailand once

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word brood is taken
the letters of the old country name are dropped from the word

parts.note: Siam was Thailand's name until 1939

explanation.surface: Neutering the final animal of a litter of Siamese kittens.
explanation.walkthrough: D + ESE (Siamese without SIAM) gives DESE; the preamble's missing X ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to remove an animal's sex organs.

clue.text: Shows respect for lethal weapons

parts.note: bowing the head shows respect

explanation.surface: Someone bowing in deference to deadly arms.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the preamble's fifteen: the word meaning angry is missing from the wordplay and goes at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval missile-firing arms that shoot bolts and can kill.

clue.text: 21 against installing electronic warning light

indicators.note: the airline's letters take in another letter

parts.note: the fliers of 21 down suggest an airline: BA is British Airways
con means against, as in pros and cons

explanation.surface: Aircraft putting in an electronic device to signal danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire lit on a hill to warn of invasion, or a signal light for ships.

clue.text: B___ sick as a parrot? No, a finch

parts.note: the letter B printed with a dash for the rest of a coy expletive is just B
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A football fan feeling bloody awful after a defeat, corrected: it is a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick as a parrot' is British football slang for bitterly disappointed. The dash stands for a coy expletive, so only its initial counts; the preamble's missing word for angry goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A finch with crossed mandible tips, used to prise seeds from pine cones.

clue.text: Refreshingly, very little said against Queen's Counsel

indicators.note: the letters are freshly arranged anew

parts.note: v is the short form of very
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A barrister, refreshingly, says little against the Crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refreshingly' rearranges V and SAID to ADVIS; 'against' joins on ER. 'Queen's Counsel' looks like a title, but 'Counsel' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister acting as counsel gives legal guidance to a client.

clue.text: Returning at first reluctantly, almost becomes part of the woodwork

indicators.note: those letters are then read backwards
the opening letters of the next three words are taken

explanation.surface: A reluctant returner who almost becomes a fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The woodwork' is football slang for the goal frame. The preamble's missing word for angry goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The horizontal beam of a football goal; hitting the frame is 'hitting the woodwork'.

clue.text: Pongs include body odour in antelopes

indicators.note: the smell's letters hold the abbreviation

parts.note: pong is British slang for stink, so pongs means reeks

explanation.surface: A grim report that some antelopes smell of sweat.
explanation.definitionFit: A South African name for small grey antelopes, also spelt rheboks.

clue.text: See spinner's over

indicators.note: the plural is turned over, read the other way

parts.note: a spinner is a top, and the 's makes it plural

explanation.surface: A cricket instruction to watch the spin bowler's set of six balls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spinner' and 'over' suggest cricket, but they are a toy and a turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to notice or catch sight of something.

clue.text: Far from comfortable, condemned characters in purdah

indicators.note: the letters are treated as wrecked, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Women in purdah, uneasy, written off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters in' joins the anagram indicator to its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: short of money, so not living comfortably.

clue.text: Stone Age tool? Joiner would be in heaven, oddly

indicators.note: the joining word goes inside the other letters
the first, third and fifth letters of the word are taken

parts.note: and is a conjunction, a joining word

explanation.surface: A carpenter thinks a primitive tool would be heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joiner' suggests a carpenter, but it is a conjunction. The preamble's missing letter shaped like a cross goes before the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehistoric flint chopper held in the hand, used in the Palaeolithic era.

clue.text: Using rifles, shot 15s, say

definitions.note: the plural stands for birds such as finches of 15 down

indicators.note: letters that are shot are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: Shooting birds with guns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' is the anagram signal, not the gunfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: finches are birds, and birds are things that fly.

clue.text: Resigns from pop group Blue

parts.note: Steps is a British pop group
feeling blue means feeling down

explanation.surface: A member quits a boy band named Blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is also a British pop group, the misdirection; here it means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to leave a position voluntarily.

clue.text: Kick out English footballer who's dropped ecstasy once

indicators.note: the footballer's name loses a letter, just one of its pair

parts.note: Pele was the Brazilian football star

indicators.note: in its abbreviated form ecstasy is just its opening letter, E, the street name for the drug

explanation.surface: An English footballer is thrown out after a drugs offence.
explanation.walkthrough: E + PEL (Pele less one E) gives EPEL; the preamble's missing X goes after the first E. 'once' stops both Es going.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to force someone to leave a school or organisation.

clue.text: Register as nurse with reduced capacity

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter

parts.note: acting in a capacity is playing a role

explanation.surface: Signing up as a nurse on part-time hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to sign on for a course or list.

clue.text: Hobnob, perhaps, as writer that is keeping the big man on board

parts.note: a Bic is a ballpoint pen
K is the king, the key piece on a chessboard
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Socialising with a writer who has the boss on the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hobnob' looks like a verb; a Hobnob is a British oat biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a Hobnob is a brand of biscuit, and this is the informal word for one.

clue.text: Point needed after City game

indicators.note: the point comes at the end, after the other letters

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
E is a compass point, east

explanation.surface: A sports team needs a point after the City match.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the preamble's fifteen: the word for a crucifix is missing from the wordplay and goes in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport played with netted sticks.

clue.text: Take stock, with unhappy result

indicators.note: the letters are unsettled and rearranged

explanation.surface: Reviewing the books after a poor outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take stock' looks like reviewing, but it means stealing livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle theft: stock here is farm animals.

clue.text: Note mistake's third to appear in clues — they're seldom spotted

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: that letter is put inside the following word
the third letter of the word mistake is taken

explanation.surface: A setter's slip shows up in a crossword's clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermits and loners avoid company, so they are rarely seen.
